title: Actions are by intentions
hook: actions are only by intentions, and each gets what he intended
tomorrow: a stranger walks in and asks what he already knows. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, arba'in: a forty that comes to forty-two, one small bag for a whole library. Forty-two foundations. The first thing in the bag is something nobody can see.

Two people stand at the same Saturday food drive, in the same aprons, stacking the same boxes. One came for the families in line. One came for the hours on a form. From the parking lot, nobody could tell them apart. Now a pulpit in Medina. Umar ibn al-Khattab stands up and repeats something he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say. It's about people on the road of the hijrah, the migration to Medina. Same road, same dust, same days of walking. And the Prophet says they didn't all arrive in the same place.
screen: `SAME APRON, SAME BOXES.` → `A PULPIT IN MEDINA.` → `SAME ROAD. DIFFERENT ARRIVALS.`

segments.voice: Here's the report, in paraphrase, as Sahih al-Bukhari opens with it: actions are only by intentions, and each person gets only what they intended. So whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger, their hijrah is for Allah and His Messenger. And whoever's hijrah was for some gain of this world, or a woman to marry, their hijrah is for what they set out for. Listen to how the sentence is built. For the first traveler, it says the goal twice, word for word. For the second, it doesn't name the goal again at all: just, what he set out for. One road, two journeys, and the difference never showed on anyone's feet. The word inside the line is niyyah, intention. One thing to tell a friend tonight: in Islamic law, intention is how one act becomes two. A bath, or the washing a Muslim does before prayer. Skipping breakfast, or a fast. From outside they look identical. The intention is what tells them apart. Al-Nawawi's bag of foundations opens here, on the part of every deed only Allah and the doer can see.
screen: `ONLY BY INTENTIONS.` · `ONE GOAL SAID TWICE, ONE NOT AGAIN.` · `NIYYAH: ONE ACT BECOMES TWO.` · `THE PART ONLY ALLAH SEES.` · then, large: `WHAT DID I INTEND?`

segments.voice: Choose the next ordinary thing you'll do after this: washing a cup, opening a laptop, calling someone back. Say quietly, in a few plain words, what you're doing it for. The intention lives in the heart; the words just help you notice it. Then sit with that one sentence for the rest of the time.
screen: `THE NEXT ORDINARY THING.` · `SAY WHAT IT'S FOR.`

segments.voice: Actions are by intentions: the opening words of al-Nawawi's first hadith. Niyyah, intention, is the word at its center, the reason one act can be two.
For the road, two seconds before anything: what did I intend? Day three of the last range, done.

screen: `DAY 1429 COUNTS.` → `YEAR FIVE · 3 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: A STRANGER WALKS IN AND ASKS WHAT HE ALREADY KNOWS. WHY?`

howItsDone: Muslims make an intention before prayer, a fast or the washing for prayer; scholars hold that it lives in the heart, and schools differ on whether to also say it quietly.

in the report, the worldly traveler's goal isn't repeated
the first goal is said twice, word for word. the second is only 'what he set out for'.

fork.setup: you volunteer at a food drive partly because it looks good on an application. a friend says that ruins it. what fits the first hadith?
options: look at what you mean by it, and set the intention before you start.
quit: if any part is for the application, none of it counts.
keep going and don't think about why: the food arrives either way.
fork.reveal: the hadith doesn't send anyone home. it says each person gets what they intended, so the first move is to look, and to set it.

original.note: Arabic: actions are only by intentions. niyyat is the plural of niyyah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice saying about meaning well.
what it means: the same act can be two acts, and each person gets what they intended.
what a scholar hears: innama, only; and a report that repeats 'Allah and His Messenger' but won't repeat the worldly goal.
guess: what you mean by a deed decides what it counts as
good actions matter more than what you meant by them
a plan only counts once you have carried it out

chat.says: real talk: am i teaching these kids for them, or bc it looks good for college? 😬
options: Look at which you mean, and set it before class. Each gets what they intended.
Once college crossed your mind it's spoiled, so honestly, step back from it.
Doesn't matter why. The kids learn the same either way, so don't overthink.
chat.meaning: Actions are by intentions, and each gets what they intended. The hadith asks you to look at your intention and set it, not to walk away.

hijrah.meaning: migration; the Prophet's move with his followers to Medina

Medina.meaning: the city in Arabia the Prophet migrated to

Umar ibn al-Khattab.meaning: a close companion of the Prophet who reported this hadith

al-Nawawi.meaning: the scholar from Syria who gathered the forty

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1 (Umar on the pulpit: actions are by intentions; the two hijrahs)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): story shape; hook opens on a food drive, then the scene on the Medina pulpit (Sahih al-Bukhari 1 begins 'I heard Umar ibn al-Khattab say on the pulpit'). Confirm the paraphrase of the hadith and the numbering (Bukhari 1, Muslim 1907).

The 'one act becomes two' examples (a bath vs ghusl/wudu; skipping breakfast vs a fast) rest on the standard fiqh requirement of niyyah for purification and fasting; schools differ on niyyah for wudu (Hanafis do not make it a condition of validity). Confirm the wording 'the washing a Muslim does before prayer' is fair, or switch to ghusl.

Practice says the intention is said quietly 'to notice it' and that it lives in the heart; schools differ on uttering the niyyah (some recommend it, others call it unneeded). howItsDone says so. Confirm.
The popular story that this hadith was occasioned by a man who migrated to marry Umm Qays is deliberately left out (its chain is discussed by scholars).
